items.sentence_raw: June 2004 saw the first passage, known as a 'transit', of the planet Venus across the face of the Sun in 122 years.
Transits have helped shape our view of the whole Universe, as Heather Cooper and Nigel Henbest explain.
On 8 June 2004, more than half the population of the world were treated to a rare astronomical event.
For over six hours, the planet Venus steadily inched its way over the surface of the Sun.
This 'transit' of Venus was the first since 6 December 1882.
On that occasion, the American astronomer Professor Simon Newcomb led a party to South Africa to observe the event.
They were based at a girl's school, where - it is alleged - the combined forces of three schoolmistresses outperformed the professionals with the accuracy of their observations.
For centuries, transits of Venus have drawn explorers and astronomers alike to the four corners of the globe.
And you can put it all down to the extraordinary polymath Edmond Halley.
In November 1677, Halley observed a transit of the innermost planet, Mercury, from the desolate island of St Helena in the south Pacific.
He realized that, from different latitudes, the passage of the planet across the Sun's disc would appear to differ.

By timing the transit from two widely-separated locations, teams of astronomers could calculate the parallax angle - the apparent difference in position of an astronomical body due to a difference in the observer's position.
items.explain: Q19: The statement says he understood the distance could be **worked out** by **comparing observations**. The passage says Halley realized *'timing the transit from two widely-separated locations'* would allow astronomers to *'measure... the distance'*. **'Two widely-separated locations'** means **comparing observations**, and **'measure'** means **worked out**. The correct person is **Edmond Halley**.

items.sentence_raw: Calculating this angle would allow astronomers to measure what was then the ultimate goal: the distance of the Earth from the sun.
items.explain: Q19: The statement says he understood the distance could be **worked out** by **comparing observations**. The passage says Halley realized *'timing the transit from two widely-separated locations'* would allow astronomers to *'measure... the distance'*. **'Two widely-separated locations'** means **comparing observations**, and **'measure'** means **worked out**. The correct person is **Edmond Halley**.

items.sentence_raw: This distance is known as the 'astronomical' or AU.
Halley was aware that the AU was one of the most fundamental of all astronomical measurements.
Johannes Kepler, in the early 17th century, had shown that the distances of the planets from the Sun governed their orbital speeds, which were easily measurable.
items.explain: Q20: The statement says he realized orbital time **depends on** distance from the Sun. The passage says Kepler showed *'distances of the planets from the Sun governed their orbital speeds'*. **'Governed'** means **depends on**, and **'orbital speeds'** relates to **time taken to go round**. The correct person is **Johannes Kepler**.

items.sentence_raw: But no-one had found a way to calculate accurate distances to the planets from the Earth.
The goal was to measure the AU; then, knowing the orbital speeds of all the other planets round the Sun, the scale of the Solar System would fall into place.
However, Halley realised that Mercury was so far away that its parallax angle would be very difficult to determine.
As Venus was closer to the Earth, its parallax angle would be larger, and Halley worked out that by using Venus it would be possible to measure the Sun's distance to 1 part in 500.
But there was a problem: transits of Venus, unlike those of Mercury, are rare, occurring in pairs roughly eight years apart every hundred or so years.
Nevertheless, he accurately predicted that Venus would cross the face of the Sun in both 1761 and 1769-though he didn't survive to see either.
items.explain: Q22: The question says Halley **observed** a Venus transit. But the passage explicitly says *'he didn't survive to see either'* of the Venus transits he predicted. ***'Didn't survive to see'*** directly contradicts **'observed'**. Therefore, the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: Inspired by Halley's suggestion of a way to pin down the scale of the Solar System, teams of British and French astronomers set out on expeditions to places as diverse as India and Siberia.
But things weren't helped by Britain and France being at war.
The person who deserves most sympathy is the French astronomer Guillaume Le Gentil.
He was thwarted by the fact that the British were besieging his observation site at Pondicherry in India.
items.explain: Q15: The question asks about an **event** that **prevented** a transit observation. The passage says Le Gentil was *'thwarted by the fact that the British were besieging his observation site'*. **'Thwarted'** means **prevented**, and **'besieging'** is the specific **event**. Therefore, the answer is **D**.

items.sentence_raw: Fleeing on a French warship crossing the Indian Ocean, Le Gentil saw a wonderful transit - but the ship's pitching and rolling ruled out any attempt at making accurate observations.
items.explain: Q21: The statement says he **witnessed** a transit but made **no calculations**. The passage says Le Gentil *'saw a wonderful transit'* but the ship's movement *'ruled out any attempt at making accurate observations'*. **'Saw'** means **witnessed**, and **'ruled out observations'** means he could not make **calculations**. The correct person is **Guillaume Le Gentil**.

items.sentence_raw: Undaunted, he remained south of the equator, keeping himself busy by studying the islands of Mauritius and Madagascar before setting off to observe the next transit in the Philippines.
Ironically after travelling nearly 50,000 kilometers, his view was clouded out at the last moment, a very dispiriting experience.
items.explain: Q23: The question claims Le Gentil **managed to observe** a second transit. However, the passage says *'his view was clouded out at the last moment'* when he tried to see the next one. ***'Clouded out'*** means he could NOT see it, which contradicts **'managed to observe'**. So the answer is **FALSE**.

items.sentence_raw: While the early transit timings were as precise as instruments would allow, the measurements were dogged by the 'black drop' effect.
When Venus begins to cross the Sun's disc, it looks smeared not circular - which makes it difficult to establish timings.
items.explain:
Q17: The question describes **physical states** of Venus that instruments could not **overcome**. The passage explains Venus *'looks smeared not circular'* and had a *'halo of light'*, making accurate timings *'impossible'*. **'Smeared'** and **'halo'** are the **physical states**, and **'impossible'** means they failed to **overcome** them. The answer is **E**.

Q24: The question says Venus appears **distorted** when it starts passing the Sun. The passage confirms that when Venus begins to cross, *'it looks smeared not circular'*. **'Smeared not circular'** is exactly what **distorted** means. Thus, the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: This is due to diffraction of light.
The second problem is that Venus exhibits a halo of light when it is seen just outside the Sun's disc.
While this showed astronomers that Venus was surrounded by thick layer of gases refracting sunlight around it, both effects made it impossible to obtain accurate timings.

items.sentence_raw: But astronomers laboured hard to analyse the results of these expeditions to observe Venus transits.
Johann Franz Encke, Director of the Berlin Observatory, finally determined a value for the AU based on all these parallax measurements: 153,340,000km.
items.explain: Q18: The statement says he **calculated** the Sun's distance with **fair accuracy**. The passage says Encke *'finally determined a value for the AU... 153,340,000km'* which was *'reasonably accurate'*. **'Determined a value'** means **calculated**, and **'reasonably accurate'** matches **fair degree of accuracy**. The correct person is **Johann Franz Encke**.

items.sentence_raw: Reasonably accurate for the time, that is quite close to today's value of methods in accuracy.
The AU is a cosmic measuring rod, and the basis of how we scale the Universe today.
items.explain: Q14: The question asks for **examples** of how the **parallax principle** is used. The passage says *'The parallax principle can be extended to measure the distances to the stars'* and mentions scaling the **Universe**. **'Extended'** means applied in **different ways**, so this matches the question perfectly. The answer is **F**.

items.sentence_raw: The parallax principle can be extended to measure the distances to the stars.

Q26: The question says the **parallax principle** helps find distances to **distant stars**. The passage clearly states *'The parallax principle can be extended to measure the distances to the stars'*. This is a direct match between the question and the text. So the answer is **TRUE**.

items.sentence_raw: If we look at a star in January - when Earth is at one point in its orbit - it will seem to be in a different position from where it appears six months later.
Knowing the width of Earth's orbit, the parallax shift lets astronomers calculate the distance.
June 2004's transit of Venus was thus more of an astronomical spectacle than a scientifically important event.
But such transits have paved the way for what might prove to be one of the most vital breakthroughs in the cosmos - detecting Earth-sized planets orbiting other stars.
items.explain: Q16: The question looks for **potential future discoveries** from transit observations. The passage states transits *'paved the way for... detecting Earth-sized planets orbiting other stars'*. **'Paved the way'** means leading to **future** results, and **'detecting planets'** are the **discoveries**. So the answer is **G**.

orphan_explain_map.25: Q25: The passage mentions Venus has a *'thick layer of gases'* but never describes the atmosphere as **toxic**. It discusses light refraction, not whether the air is poisonous or safe. Since the text neither confirms nor denies if it is **toxic**, the answer is **NOT GIVEN**. ***NOT GIVEN means the information is missing, not wrong***.
